storm.summary_layperson: A slight chance of an isolated shower before 8pm, otherwise a quiet, dry evening with no thunderstorm risk in sight for the cove.
storm.local_effect_blurb: The Sound's usual cooling buffer is already gone for the evening — air and water are within about 5°F of each other at 6 PM and the air keeps cooling past that afterward, but with no storms in the pipeline it doesn't matter tonight.
storm.detail_html:
Long Island Sound is quiet tonight. KOKX radar shows no echoes approaching the area, there are no active NWS watches or advisories, and instability is modest — CAPE runs 590–1430 J/kg through the 18:00–22:00 window, staying under the 1500 J/kg punch-through gate even with a healthy 34 kt of deep-layer shear aloft. The National Weather Service carries only a 20% chance of a shower before 8 PM, then partly cloudy skies.

The cove's usual storm-taming trick — the cool Sound water creating a stable marine layer that chokes off incoming cells — isn't available tonight regardless. The air–water gap is already down to about 5°F at 6 PM (water 76°F, air 81°F) and keeps shrinking as the evening air cools, going slightly negative (air cooler than water) by 8 PM. That's below the roughly 5°F threshold this mechanism needs to do meaningful work.

None of this matters much tonight simply because there's nothing on radar to blunt. The most likely outcome for the cove is the same as everywhere else nearby: dry, partly cloudy, with only a small chance of a passing light shower in the first hour or two of the window.

What would change the call: any new cell development on KOKX radar, an updated Area Forecast Discussion flagging expanding shower coverage, or CAPE building past 1500 J/kg with shear holding — none of which is forecast through 22:00 tonight.

wind.tactics_blurb: Light gradient flow tonight, not a sea-breeze day — starts SE/SSE and veers to SSW/SW through the window, mostly 4–8 kt. Play the middle of the course early while it's shifty and light, favoring the west side if Tod's Point shadow shows up; expect a modest fill and steadier SSW-SW pressure by 20:00–22:00.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
Today doesn't clear the thermal gate: the air–water temperature difference is 4.7°F, just under the 5°F threshold this skill uses to call a sea breeze, and the western-LIS station cluster is only 45% southerly — not the confident majority a mature sea breeze usually shows. With the thermal ingredient missing, this is classified a gradient-only day, and the region's authoritative (airport-grade) wind average of 5.8 kt keeps it in the light sub-class: no sea breeze, direction driven by whatever weak synoptic flow is around, not the sun.

There's a real HRRR/observation split worth flagging: the model has the window starting at SE (136°) and slowly veering to SW by 22:00, but Riverside YC is currently reading NW at 4.4 kt (gusting 9.1) while the broader western-LIS ensemble median is already SW (214°) — a 78° gap between model and obs. Because today doesn't qualify as a sea-breeze day, the maturation correction this skill normally applies on thermal days isn't triggered, so the hourly table below uses the raw HRRR progression. Treat the early-window direction with caution — it may already be more SW than the model shows.

Cove geography: SE/SSE flow (the modeled early hours) gets partial shelter from Greenwich Point, favoring the west side of the course with lighter, shiftier air near Tod's Point. By the time flow backs into SSW/SW later in the window, the cove sees fairly uniform pressure with maybe a touch more strength near the mouth and east shore. That transition argues against committing hard to one side — start in the middle, lean west early, and expect the course to even out as the direction settles SW.

Speed-wise this is a drifter-to-light-air window: 3–8 kt for most of the five hours, dipping into borderline no-race territory in the first hour or two before firming up slightly around 20:00. RYC's own gust spread (more than double the sustained speed right now) suggests puffy, inconsistent pressure rather than smooth flow — sailors should expect the fleet to bunch and separate on gusts rather than see clean, predictable shifts.
